summary: Defines a generic notification message for Mobile IPv4, letting mobility entities send and receive explicit notifications using a message type made for the purpose. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for the helpers that keep a moving phone connected to send each other short messages saying that something happened.

questions: what is a mobile ipv4 generic notification message
what is a gnam in mobile ip
how does mobile ipv4 prevent notification replay
what is the md field in mobile ipv4 notification
subtitle: Lets Mobile IPv4 nodes send each other unsolicited, acknowledged notifications, such as billing or service messages.

tldr.problem: Base Mobile IPv4 has no way for a home agent, foreign agent or mobile node to send an asynchronous message during a mobility session, that is, one not tied to a Registration Request or Reply.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Generic Notification Message (type 22) and a Generic Notification Acknowledgement Message (type 23), authenticated with the existing Mobile IPv4 authentication extensions and protected against replay by the Identification field.
tldr.outcome: On its own it can carry only a text Message String Extension, which has no effect on a registration. It is a Proposed Standard and a base for later notification extensions.

today: RFC 6098 is a Proposed Standard from April 2012. It is not obsoleted or updated by any RFC listed in its metadata.

sections.title: The Missing Notification Channel
sections.content:
In Mobile IPv4, a mobile node (MN) keeps its connectivity as it moves, with help from a home agent (HA) and sometimes a foreign agent (FA). The base specification, RFC 5944, only has messages that are synchronous with the Registration Request and Registration Reply. It has no provision for asynchronous messages during a mobility session.

RFC 6098 fills that gap with two new messages: the Generic Notification Message (GNM) and the Generic Notification Acknowledgement Message (GNAM). The acknowledgement makes reliable delivery possible.

Only four extensions may appear in these messages: the MN-HA, MN-FA and FA-HA Authentication Extensions, and the Message String Extension from RFC 4917. Receiving a GNM with a Message String Extension has null semantics: it has no effect on the state of the mobile node's existing registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this, the helpers of a moving phone could only chat during check-ins. Now they can send a short note whenever something happens, and the receiver can say thanks.

sections.title: Who Notifies Whom
sections.content:
The simplest use is a message that is only displayed to a user or operator. The RFC gives examples such as a warning that a prepaid quota is nearly used up, a note that spending passed a notification threshold, or a message about a service interruption. These work with the Message String Extension alone.

Other uses need extensions that this document does not define. The RFC lists HA switch-over, Network Mobility prefix changes, load balancing, service termination and service interruption. It notes that Registration Revocation (RFC 3543) would have been better defined as a notification with a revocation extension.

Notifications can flow between an HA and an MN, an FA and an MN, or an HA and an FA. When the mobile node uses a foreign agent care-of address, the HA cannot reach the MN directly, so the FA relays the message. With a co-located care-of address the HA and MN talk directly. The mechanism does not support a co-located care-of address with registration through an FA.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes can go between any two of the three helpers. If the phone is behind a middleman, the middleman passes the note along.

sections.title: The GNM and GNAM Formats
sections.content:
Both messages travel over UDP and reuse the IP addresses and UDP ports of the last Registration Request or Reply between the same two entities. This helps NAT traversal and keeps the same security association as registration. The node sending a GNM follows the same procedure as for sending a Registration Request.

The GNM starts with Type 22, a one-byte MD (Message Direction) field, and an A bit. If A is 1, acknowledgement is REQUIRED; if 0, it is OPTIONAL. Next come the Home Address, Home Agent Address, Care-of Address and a 64-bit Identification, followed by extensions.

The GNAM uses Type 23 and replaces the A bit with a Code that reports the result. The MD values are 0 (HA to MN), 1 (HA to FA), 2 (MN to HA), 3 (MN to FA), 4 (FA to MN) and 5 (FA to HA).

Code 0 means accepted. Denials use separate ranges: 64 to 69 from the FA, 128 to 133 from the HA and 192 to 197 from the MN. Within each range the reasons are unspecified, administratively prohibited, insufficient resources, two kinds of failed authentication, and Identification mismatch.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has a label saying who it is from and who it is for, and whether a reply is needed. The reply carries a number: zero for fine, other numbers for the reason it was turned down.

sections.title: How Each Node Handles Messages
sections.content:
Each node type has detailed rules. A receiver MUST check the authentication extension that fits the MD value. The required one is MN-HA between MN and HA, MN-FA between MN and FA, and FA-HA between FA and HA. It MUST also check the Identification and that only permitted extensions are present. An MN, FA or HA that rejects a GNM for failed authentication or a bad Identification MAY send a GNAM with the matching error Code and SHOULD log a security exception. A message with a non-permitted extension is silently discarded.

The FA also relays messages between MN and HA while it holds a binding for the MN. A relaying FA MUST NOT modify the fixed portion of the message through the authorization-enabling authentication extension. It processes and removes later extensions and may append its own, followed by its authentication extension if it shares a security association.

An HA that receives a GNM from an FA with no matching MN registration SHOULD drop it. If the A flag is set on a GNM from an FA or an MN, the HA MUST send a GNAM. Unacknowledged GNMs SHOULD be retransmitted. The minimum time between GNMs MUST NOT be less than 1 second, and each retransmission timeout SHOULD be at least twice the previous one.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone checks the stamp on a note before believing it. Middlemen pass it on without changing the important part, and a note that fails the check is thrown away.

sections.title: Extending the Notification Message
sections.content:
The RFC expects new notification-related extensions for content meant for the HA, FA or MN rather than a human user. Examples it names are Registration Revocation, managed switch-over between HA instances, load balancing, a Network Mobility prefix change (RFC 5177) and home network changes such as a new DNS server address.

To keep the GNM from becoming an unreviewed way to add protocol features, any new extension permitted for use with it must be defined in an RFC under the 'RFC Required' policy. The notion of skippable and non-skippable extensions from RFC 5944 still applies, and a non-skippable extension that is not recognized means the message is silently discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The note format is like an envelope that other documents can fill with new kinds of letters, but every new kind needs an official RFC first.

sections.title: Authentication and Replay Protection
sections.content:
A GNM could carry information that modifies mobility bindings, so it MUST be integrity protected and replay protection MUST be guaranteed. RFC 5944 gives replay protection only for Registration Requests sent by the MN, so this RFC uses the 64-bit Identification field for notifications started by an FA or HA.

Two methods exist. Support for timestamps is REQUIRED and support for nonces is OPTIONAL. The two peers MUST agree on one as part of the mobility security association. With timestamps the field holds an NTP-format value (RFC 5905) that MUST be greater than any earlier GNM. A default tolerance of 7 seconds MAY be used, and it SHOULD be greater than 3 seconds. With nonces, the receiver puts a fresh random value in the high-order 32 bits of each GNAM and the sender echoes it in its next GNM.

In both methods the low-order 32 bits are copied unchanged from GNM to GNAM and used to match them. If a timestamp is invalid, the GNAM carries Code 69, 133 or 197 and the receiver's own time so the sender can resynchronize. If an FA shares no security association with the MN or HA, non-authentication extensions it relays are unprotected and should be silently discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note gets a number that must be newer than the last one, like a ticket number. A copied old note has an old ticket number, so it is rejected.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The two new message numbers come from the same number space as the Registration Request and Registration Reply messages. IANA added a column to the registry of Mobile IPv4 extensions saying whether each extension is permitted with the GNM; four are permitted.

The Code field gets a new number space: 0 for success, 64 to 69 for FA errors, 128 to 133 for HA errors and 192 to 197 for MN errors. New Code values need expert review.
sections.plainLanguage: The message types and reply codes get official numbers, like room numbers in a building, so nobody reuses them by accident.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: 1 means acknowledgement is REQUIRED; 0 means OPTIONAL.

fields.name: Home Address
fields.desc: Home address of the mobile node.

fields.name: Home Agent Address
fields.desc: IP address of the mobile node's HA.

fields.name: Care-of Address
fields.desc: Co-located or foreign agent care-of address.

fields.name: Identification
fields.desc: Matches GNM to GNAM and protects against replay.
